summary_html: Agency decides to **remove a child immediately** due to **imminent danger** prior to a court order. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) requires later **court findings** on reasonable efforts; constitutional limits (due process; search/seizure) apply.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — monitors safety & removal decision quality

provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: In a § 1983 suit arising from an Arkansas DHS/State Police removal, the court held that the removal of children requires reasonable suspicion of child abuse, that the officials here had it, and that they were therefore entitled to qualified immunity.
key_cases.relevance: It is the leading circuit authority for evaluating an emergency-removal decision made by Arkansas DHS and State Police without prior judicial authorization.
key_cases.quote: it is clearly established that the removal of children from their parents' custody violates a constitutional right if the removal occurs without reasonable suspicion of child abuse

key_cases.case_name: Heartland Academy Community Church v. Waddle
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed declaratory and injunctive relief, holding that a juvenile officer's mass removal of boarding students on stale ex parte orders or on no order at all, without exigent circumstances or notice and hearing, violated the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments.
key_cases.relevance: It shows that even a facially valid ex parte order will not save a removal decision if it was obtained on stale or inaccurate information and no exigency existed.
key_cases.quote: The problem here is that Waddle effected the wholesale removal of HCA's boarding students with ex parte orders or no orders at all in the absence of exigent circumstances.

key_cases.case_name: Mitchell v. Dakota County Social Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that removal supported by reasonable suspicion of child abuse, followed by a petition and hearing within days, violated neither substantive nor procedural due process, and the caseworkers had qualified immunity.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Eighth Circuit's articulation of how quickly the emergency-removal decision must be tested in court, the federal analogue to Arkansas's five-business-day probable-cause hearing under Ark. Code Ann. § 9-27-315.
key_cases.quote: In child removal cases, the meaningful time and manner requirement means that the state must hold a hearing promptly after removal.

key_cases.case_name: Arkansas Department of Human Services v. Cox
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the Arkansas guardianship orders and held that DHS had no authority to seize a newborn on a Florida ex parte order that had never been registered or enforced through an Arkansas court.
key_cases.relevance: It is the clearest Arkansas Supreme Court rebuke of an emergency seizure taken without lawful authority.
key_cases.quote: DHS is utterly without authority to execute an order from a foreign jurisdiction on its own.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of qualified immunity on a motion to dismiss, holding that an Arkansas State Police Crimes Against Children Division investigator who participated in removing seven children from their Hot Springs home could be liable because the complaint plausibly alleged she acted without reasonable suspicion of child abuse.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Eighth Circuit's fullest treatment of an Arkansas emergency-removal decision made at the close of a search, and it allowed the family's claim to proceed past qualified immunity.
key_cases.quote: whether there was reasonable suspicion of child abuse warranting removal must be determined by analyzing the totality of the circumstances at the time of the removal

state_agency.name: Arkansas Department of Human Services, Division of Children and Family Services

timeline_requirements.deadline: 45 days to make the investigative determination; one 15-day extension permitted (60 days maximum)
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Receipt of the child maltreatment report from the Child Abuse Hotline (9 CAR § 40-324(a))
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Ark. Code Ann. § 12-18-616(a)(2): the timing requirement "shall not be considered as a factor to alter the investigative determination in any judicial or administrative proceeding"
